title: Z-Score Neurofeedback
subtitle: Real-time comparison with a normative model
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating z-score neurofeedback within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain z-score neurofeedback without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in z-score neurofeedback.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to z-score neurofeedback.

sections.explainSimply: Z-score systems compare selected EEG features with a normative database and may reward movement toward the reference range.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: A z-score describes statistical distance under specific acquisition and processing assumptions; it does not diagnose or define an optimal state.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Multivariate and “live” z-score systems can train many features simultaneously, complicating contingency, causal interpretation and replication.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Choosing a camera lens: every method emphasises some information and introduces its own distortions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand z-score neurofeedback to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Normalising numbers is not the same as improving the person.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using z-score neurofeedback predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Normalising numbers is not the same as improving the person. Evidence classification: emerging; mixed and limited controlled evidence.
